modules.name: Analysis of Chemical Composition and primary and secondary Metabolite

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.text:
Biomolecules: All the organic compounds/molecules that can be obtained from a living cell/tissue/organism are known as biomolecules include carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids.
• If we perform an analysis of a plant tissue, animal tissue or a microbial paste, Carbon, Hydrogen, Oxygen and several other elements are obtained.
• The same analysis made on a non-living matter like a piece of Earth's crust, gives a list of similar chemicals.

blocks.title: How to Analyse Chemical Composition?
blocks.text:
1. Analysis of organic compounds :

• Lipids are not strictly macromolecules. Because their molecular weight do not exceed 800 Da, but they come under the macromolecular fraction because when we grind a tissue, cell membrane and other membranes are broken into pieces and form vesicles which are not water soluble (lipids are also present in structures like cell membrane and other membranes).

• Lipids are not strictly macromolecules. Because their molecular weight do not exceed 800 Da, but they come under the macromolecular fraction because when we grind a tissue, cell membrane and other membranes are broken into pieces and form vesicles which are not water soluble (lipids are also present in structures like cell membrane and other membranes).

2. Analysis of inorganic elements and compounds :

• Inorganic elements and compounds are also present in the living organisms which can be known with the help of 'Ash' analysis technique.
• A small amount of a living tissue (e.g. Leaf or liver) is weighed (this is called wet weight) and dried. All the water evaporates.
• When the tissue is fully burnt, the Carbon compounds are oxidised to gaseous form like CO₂, water vapour are removed and the remnant is called 'Ash'. This ash contains many inorganic elements like Calcium,Magnesium etc.

blocks.title: 1. Chemical Analysis
blocks.text: • It gives an idea of the kind of organic and inorganic constituents present in living tissues.

blocks.title: Metabolites (NCERT table)
blocks.text:
• The acid soluble pool contains chemicals with small molecular mass of 18-800 daltons approximately. They are called micromolecules or biomicromolecules.
    • The acid-insoluble fraction contains organic compounds that have molecular weights in the range of ten thousand daltons and above. They are known as macromolecules or biomacromolecules. They include polysaccharides, proteins, nucleic acids.

blocks.title: Primary & Secondary Metabolites
blocks.text:
Metabolites : Metabolites are the intermediate products of metabolism.

NOTE : Thus, primary metabolites have identifiable (Recognizable) functions and play known roles in normal physiological processes. The functions or role of secondary metabolites in host organisms are not understood. However, many of them are useful to human welfare (e.g., rubber, drugs, spices, scents and pigments) and also have ecological importance.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Monomer vs. Polymer Confusion: Monomers are single units; polymers are multiple monomers.
      • Neglecting Functional Groups: Leads to misunderstandings of molecular properties.
      • Misinterpreting Formulas: Accurate molecular formula representation is crucial.
      • Misconception: Secondary metabolites are not less important despite being non-essential; they have crucial ecological roles.
      • Error in Examples: Do not confuse primary and secondary metabolites; categorize based on necessity and function.
      • Overlooking Roles: Recognize the ecological significance of secondary metabolites for plant adaptations and interactions.

blocks.title: Amino acids
blocks.text:
Amino acids are organic compounds containing an amino group and an acidic group as substituents on the same carbon i.e., the $\alpha$-carbon. Hence, they are called  $\alpha$-amino acids. They are substituted methanes. There are four substituent groups occupying the four valency positions.

• Each amino acid is amphoteric compound because it contains both acidic - (COOH) and an alkaline group - $\mathbf{\mathrm{NH}_2}$

• Ionic structure of AA depends on pH of medium.

blocks.title: Carbohydrates
blocks.text:
• Primary respiratory substrate - carbohydrate
    • Compounds of Carbon, Hydrogen and Oxygen with ratio of H and 0 is 2: 1, so they are also called as Hydrates of Carbon.
    • Generalised formula of carbohydrates is $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{x}}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_{\mathrm{y}}$.
    • Chemically all carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones.

blocks.text: They are simplest sugars which cannot be further hydrolysed.

Disaccharides
blocks.text:
Maltose - Maltose is commonly called malt sugar. It is intermediate compound in starch digestion. Maltose is more abundant in germinating starchy seeds.

Lactose- Lactose is milk sugar Lactose is least sweet sugar. Maximum % of lactose in human milk $\approx 7$

Sucrose: In plants, transport of sugars mainly occurs in the form of sucrose. Sucrose is also known as Invert sugar. Sucrose is called Cane Sugar or Table Sugar or Commercial Sugar.

blocks.title: Points to be Remembered
blocks.text:
• All monosaccharides are reducing in nature.
    • Some disaccharides/oligosaccharides are reducing in nature while others are non-reducing in nature. (Sucrose and Trehalose)
    • All polysaccharides are non-reducing in nature.

blocks.title: Polysaccharides
blocks.text:
• Polysaccharides are composed of large number of monosaccharide units.
    • Polysaccharides are insoluble in water and do not taste sweet.
    • All polysaccharide are non-reducing but in a polysaccharide chain, the right end is called the reducing end and the left end is called the non-reducing end.
    • According to function, they are classified as nutritive and structural.

blocks.title: Glycogen
blocks.text:
• Storage form of carbohydrate in animals, storage region of glycogen is liver and muscles. Storage of glycogen liver > muscles.
    • Glycogen is also called as animal starch. Glycogen is highly branched polymer of $\alpha$-D-glucose. It is made up of approximately $\mathbf{6 , 0 0 , 0 0 0} \alpha$-D-Glucose units.
    • Glycogen has 1'-4" glycosidic linkage at long chain and 1'-6" glycosidic linkage at branching point. Branching occurs at approximately 8-12 glucose units.

blocks.title: Saturated Fatty Acids & Unsaturated Fatty Acids

rows: (a) Only single bonds are present between C-C atoms
(a) Double bonds are also present with single bonds between C-C atoms.
(b) Also known as non-essential fatty acids, because they can be synthesized in animal body, so it is not essential to take them with food.
(b) Also known as essential fatty acids because they can't be synthesised in animal body, so it is essential to take them with food.
(c) Lipids with more amounts of saturated fatty acids are mostly present in solid form at normal temperature, e.g. Butter, Ghee
(c) Lipids with more amounts of unsaturated fatty acids are mostly present in liquid form at normal temperature, e.g. Coconut oil, Mustard oil.

(d) Metabolically they are very less reactive. So mostly don't participate in metabolism. So have tendency to store in animal body and cause obesity. Some amount of saturated fatty acids convert into cholesterol in liver. This cholesterol is deposited on inner wall of blood vessels, so cause high blood pressure & different types of cardio-vascular diseases.

(d) Metabolically they are highly reactive, so mostly participate in metabolic reactions. So don't have tendency to store in animal body. So no obesity, no cholesterol formation, no cardiovascular disease, no high B.P. & no harmful effect.
(e) Mostly animal fat contains high amount of saturated fatty acids.
(e) Mostly plant fat contains high amount of unsaturated fatty acids.

blocks.title: Enzymes
blocks.text:
• Enzymes are biocatalyst.
• Almost all enzymes are proteins.
• Some enzymes are nucleic acids (RNA), called Ribozymes.
• Enzymes can be depicted by a line diagram.
• Any enzyme like any protein has the primary, secondary & tertiary structure.
• Catalytic structure of most of the enzymes is tertiary.
• Inorganic catalysts work efficiently at high temperatures and high pressures while enzymes get damaged at high temperatures (above 40°C)
• Enzymes of thermophilic organisms have thermal stability i.e. they retain their catalytic power even at high temperatures (upto 80°-90°C)
• A general rule of thumb is that rate of any reaction doubles or decreases by half for every 10°C change in either direction.
• Enzymes are very specific to their substrate.
• Turn over number : Number of substrate molecules  converted into products per unit time.
• Carbonic anhydrase has turn over number 6,00000/sec.

blocks.title: Concept of Activation Energy
blocks.text:
The difference in average energy content of substrate from that of transition state is called activation energy.

• Enzymes bring down activation energy.

• During any enzymatic reaction, formation of enzyme-substrate complex is an obligatory and transient phenomenon.

blocks.title: Nature of Enzyme Action
blocks.text:
Substrate binds to the active site of enzyme, fitting into the active site.
                                                            ↓
The binding of the substrate induces the enzyme to alter its shape, fitting more tightly around the substrate.[ES complex]
                                                            ↓
Active site of enzyme comes in close proximity of the substrate and breaks or form the chemical bonds of substrate. Enzyme-product complex [EP] is formed.
                                                            ↓
Enzyme releases the product and gets free to bind to another substrate
Enzyme + Substrate $\rightleftharpoons[E S] \rightarrow[E P] \rightarrow$ Enzyme + Product

blocks.title: Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity
blocks.text:
1. Temperature:

2. pH:

3. Change in substrate concentration:

4. INHIBITORS :
    • The activity of an enzyme is sensitive to specific chemical that binds to enzyme.
    • Competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate in its molecular structure.
    • Competitive inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site of enzyme.
    • Malonate is competitive inhibitor of succinate for succinate dehydrogenase
    • Competitive inhibitors are often used in the control of bacterial pathogens.
Km-value : The concentration of substrate at which rate of reaction attains half of its maximum velocity.

    • Low temperature preserves the enzyme in a temporarily inactive state whereas high temperature destroys enzymatic activity because proteins are denatured by heat.

blocks.title: Co-Factors
blocks.text:
Holoenzyme = Apoenzyme (Protein part) + Co-factor(Non-protein part)
    • Non-protein constituent of enzyme required to make it catalytically active is called cofactor.
    • Catalytic activity is lost when co-factor is removed from the enzyme which testifies that they play a crucial role in the catalytic activity of the enzyme.

1. Co-enzyme:
    • They are organic compounds
    • They are loosely bound to apoenzyme.
    • Association with apoenzyme is transient.
    • The essential components of many coenzymes are vitamins.
    • Co-enzyme Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) and NADP contain vitamin niacin.

2. Prosthetic Group:
    • They are organic or inorganic compounds.
    • They are tightly bound to apoenzyme.
    • In peroxidase and catalase, which catalyze the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) to water and oxygen, haem is the prosthetic group and it is a part of the active site of the enzyme.

3. Metal Ion:
    • Loosely attached inorganic co-factor.
    • Form coordination bonds with side chains at active site and at the same time form one or more coordination bonds with the substrate.
    • Zn is metal ion co-factor for the proteolytic enzyme carboxy-peptidase.

• Monomer vs. Polymer Confusion: Monomers are single units; polymers are multiple monomers.
      • Neglecting Functional Groups: Leads to misunderstandings of molecular properties.
      • Misinterpreting Formulas: Accurate molecular formula representation is crucial.
      • Misconception: Secondary metabolites are not less important despite being non-essential; they have crucial ecological roles.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Base Pairing Errors: Confusing base pairing rules (e.g., pairing adenine with cytosine instead of thymine).
  • DNA and RNA Differences: Misunderstanding structural and functional differences.
  • Replication vs. Transcription: Mixing up processes and enzymes involved.
  • Central Dogma Misinterpretation: Confusing the direction of information flow.
  • Chargaff's Rule Misapplication: Forgetting rule applies only to DNA, not RNA.

blocks.title: Amino acids
blocks.text:
Amino acids are organic compounds containing an amino group and an acidic group as substituents on the same carbon i.e., the $\alpha$-carbon. Hence, they are called  $\alpha$-amino acids. They are substituted methanes. There are four substituent groups occupying the four valency positions.

• Each amino acid is amphoteric compound because it contains both acidic - (COOH) and an alkaline group - $\mathbf{\mathrm{NH}_2}$

• Ionic structure of AA depends on pH of medium.

Maltose - Maltose is commonly called malt sugar. It is intermediate compound in starch digestion. Maltose is more abundant in germinating starchy seeds.

Lactose- Lactose is milk sugar Lactose is least sweet sugar. Maximum % of lactose in human milk $\approx 7$

Sucrose: In plants, transport of sugars mainly occurs in the form of sucrose. Sucrose is also known as Invert sugar. Sucrose is called Cane Sugar or Table Sugar or Commercial Sugar.

blocks.title: Concept of Activation Energy
blocks.text:
The difference in average energy content of substrate from that of transition state is called activation energy.

• Enzymes bring down activation energy.

• During any enzymatic reaction, formation of enzyme-substrate complex is an obligatory and transient phenomenon.

Saturated Fatty Acids & Unsaturated Fatty Acids

rows: (a) Only single bonds are present between C-C atoms
(a) Double bonds are also present with single bonds between C-C atoms.
(b) Also known as non-essential fatty acids, because they can be synthesized in animal body, so it is not essential to take them with food.
(b) Also known as essential fatty acids because they can't be synthesised in animal body, so it is essential to take them with food.
(c) Lipids with more amounts of saturated fatty acids are mostly present in solid form at normal temperature, e.g. Butter, Ghee
(c) Lipids with more amounts of unsaturated fatty acids are mostly present in liquid form at normal temperature, e.g. Coconut oil, Mustard oil.

(d) Metabolically they are very less reactive. So mostly don't participate in metabolism. So have tendency to store in animal body and cause obesity. Some amount of saturated fatty acids convert into cholesterol in liver. This cholesterol is deposited on inner wall of blood vessels, so cause high blood pressure & different types of cardio-vascular diseases.

(d) Metabolically they are highly reactive, so mostly participate in metabolic reactions. So don't have tendency to store in animal body. So no obesity, no cholesterol formation, no cardiovascular disease, no high B.P. & no harmful effect.
(e) Mostly animal fat contains high amount of saturated fatty acids.
(e) Mostly plant fat contains high amount of unsaturated fatty acids.
